clue.text: Vineyard can be found close to the coast

parts.note: cru is the word for a vineyard on a French wine label, as in grand cru
what a thing can be, it is, and those two letters are that little verb written out

indicators.note: The close of a thing is where it stops, so all that is taken from the word after it is the letter it ends on.

parts.note: the letter that small word finishes on

explanation.surface: A vineyard lying a short way inland from the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to the coast' reads as one phrase and splits in two, the last word of it doing the defining. 'Coast' is the verb there, not the shoreline the vineyard overlooks.
explanation.definitionFit: To coast is to keep moving along without effort, which is what a car or a candidate is doing when it cruises.

clue.text: Make light of dropping Penny's cushion on the floor

indicators.note: Dropping a thing lets it fall away, so the letter named next is gone from the word holding it.

parts.note: to underplay a problem is to make light of it
p is the penny of a price tag, the coin cut down to one letter

explanation.surface: Treating the knocking of Penny's cushion onto the floor as nothing much.
explanation.walkthrough: Penny is a woman in the surface and a coin in the wordplay, and 'dropping' is an instruction rather than what happened to the cushion. The definition is the last four words.
explanation.definitionFit: An underlay is the springy sheet laid beneath a carpet, so it really is the cushion between you and the floorboards.

clue.text: Queen carrying long stick flipped runner off

indicators.note: A porter walks under the load, so in a down clue the one doing the carrying has her letters below the thing carried.
A flipped pancake comes down the other way up, so the word it touches is written from its last letter back.

parts.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the monogram on a British postbox
a pole is the long stick, and its four letters run the other way here

explanation.surface: A queen swinging a long staff and flipping a carpet runner off the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue whoever is carrying something stands beneath it, which is why the queen's two letters finish the answer. 'Runner' sounds athletic and means somebody who runs off, usually to be married.
explanation.definitionFit: To elope is to run off to marry without permission, so the one who does it is a runner off in the plainest sense.

clue.text: European rocket chicks regularly brought up in chitchat

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing up means reading the letters from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to rocket is to zoom upwards

indicators.note: taking every other letter of chicks, starting with the second

explanation.surface: A European space rocket's young birds are discussed in casual talk.
explanation.walkthrough: Every second letter of chicks gives HCS; E, ZOOM and HCS together are then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To schmooze is to chat in a cosy, ingratiating way, a sort of small talk or chitchat.

clue.text: English teacher missing end of term, for a festival

parts.note: e is English on a school timetable or a dictionary label

indicators.note: Somebody missing is not where they should be, so the letter named next is absent from the word it belongs to.

parts.note: a schoolmaster is a teacher, the word still used at many British schools
the last letter of 'term', which is what the teacher goes without

explanation.surface: An English teacher slipping away before the end of term for a holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of term' is the school holidays in the surface and one letter in the wordplay. 'Master' is the school word for a teacher, and it is what makes the deletion available at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is the spring festival of the Christian year, so 'a festival' names it by the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Tighten Geraint's wheels

indicators.note: To wheel is to turn about on the spot, and a word turned about comes out with its letters in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Somebody tightening the wheels on Geraint's bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: Geraint Thomas is the Welsh rider who won the Tour de France, which is why wheels follow the name so naturally. The answer is the verb behind astringent, the lotion that draws the skin tight.
explanation.definitionFit: To astringe is to draw something tight or constrict it, so it is 'tighten' in a medical register.

clue.text: Slight difficulties if Romeo cracks shellfish

indicators.note: To crack a thing open is to make a way into it, so the letter named before goes inside the word that follows.

parts.note: winkles are the little sea snails picked out of their shells with a pin
Romeo is R in the radio alphabet that starts Alpha, Bravo, Charlie

explanation.surface: Romeo running into trouble the moment he starts cracking shellfish open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Romeo' is the radio alphabet's R rather than the lover, and that is the whole of the disguise. A wrinkle in a plan is a small snag, not a crease.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrinkles are the small snags left in a scheme — the ones still to be ironed out — which is slight difficulties in the plural.

clue.text: England at that point during series toughening up

indicators.note: Anything that happens during a match happens inside it, so the letters named before are written within the word after.

parts.note: a string of defeats is a series of them
Eng is how a scoreboard shortens England
at that point in the story means then

explanation.surface: England growing harder to beat as the Test series goes on.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cricket series England are growing into, and 'series' is quietly the ordinary word for any run of things. 'At that point' is four letters of plain English hiding as a phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Strengthening is growing stronger, and a side toughening up is doing exactly that in the language of sport.

clue.text: Long seat in church aisle needing length

parts.note: ch is the church of a street map and a parish noticeboard

indicators.note: A word needing something has not got it, so the letter named at the end is the one absent from the word before.

parts.note: the word is taken whole before anything comes out of it
l is length in a formula, sitting beside w for width

explanation.surface: A church aisle that wants more length, with a long seat standing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Furniture and architecture sit together so comfortably that nothing announces 'needing' as an instruction. The answer is the first word of chaise longue, doing the job on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaise is the long low seat you stretch out on, English having shortened chaise longue to its first word.

clue.text: Rent more than it was reported

indicators.note: Something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so what counts is the noise the words make rather than their spelling.

parts.note: a price more than it was is higher, and that comparative said aloud is what gets written down

explanation.surface: A rent that has gone up since last time, by all accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: Rent and the answer are the same transaction seen from either side of the counter. The clue's 'it' is the rent itself, which is what keeps four words reading as one sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To hire a thing is to pay for the use of it for a while, which is what 'rent' says when you are the one paying.

clue.text: Bossy politician to the right behind Macron's dad

indicators.note: Whatever stands behind another thing comes after it, so the two pieces named first are written last.

parts.note: père is French for father, and the French president is there to signal the language
an MP is the politician who sits in the House of Commons
the Tories are the party of the right in British politics

explanation.surface: A domineering right-wing MP standing behind Macron's father.
explanation.walkthrough: Macron is in the clue for the French, not the politics: his 'dad' is père, the accent dropped as crosswords always drop them. Britain's party of the right supplies the last four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A peremptory order is one that allows no discussion and expects no refusal, which is bossiness at its most clipped.

clue.text: Old dog on film is one that howls

definitions.meaning: the stray that the boy takes in, in the Disney picture of 1957 that every American child was made to watch
the agent noun built straight off the verb: somebody who yells

explanation.surface: An ageing film dog that will not stop howling.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are about the same animal, which is why the join is invisible: the film's title carries 'old' as its first word. The second definition spells the noise differently from the way it is usually spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Yeller is the yellow stray of the Disney film, named for the noise he makes, and a yeller is anyone who yells or howls.

clue.text: Rubber lips for notable work by Magritte, say

indicators.note: the lips of a word are its edges, its first and last letters

parts.note: the word whose two edge letters are used
op, short for opus, is a work
René Magritte was the Belgian surrealist painter; he is one example of a man with this first name

explanation.surface: A painting of rubbery lips, presented as a celebrated Magritte.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lips for' gives NE, the edges of notable; Magritte is just one bearer of the first name, hence 'say'. Magritte did paint lips, which is the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Neoprene is a synthetic rubber used for wetsuits and laptop sleeves.

clue.text: Naughty ad by telephone not acceptable

indicators.note: Naughty children do not do as they are told, and letters that will not behave come out in an order nobody asked for.

parts.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A smutty advertisement placed over the telephone that nobody should have taken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naughty' does double duty, describing the ad and shuffling the letters, which is why the sentence runs so smoothly. The pale was the fenced boundary of English rule around Dublin, and outside it lay everything unruly.
explanation.definitionFit: To be beyond the pale is to be outside the bounds of what people will put up with, the pale being that fence, so it says plainly not acceptable.

clue.text: Extremely good-looking NI footballer keeps playing there

indicators.note: A goalkeeper keeps what comes at him, so the name before this word holds the letters after it inside.

parts.note: George Best of Northern Ireland, the Manchester United winger of the sixties
a show playing tonight is on tonight
'there' points back at Northern Ireland, whose two letters are already printed in the clue

explanation.surface: A strikingly handsome Northern Irish footballer who still turns out at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There' sends you back to Northern Ireland, so those two letters do duty twice over — once to name the player, once as themselves. Bonny is the Scots and northern word for good-looking.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonny is the Scots and northern English word for good-looking, so its superlative is the extreme of it.

clue.text: Carrying blade, wandering Genoa's dangerous neighbourhood

indicators.note: What you are carrying travels with you, so the letters named first go into the mix along with the rest.
A wanderer keeps to no set route, and letters that wander finish up somewhere other than where they started.

parts.note: a rower's blade is the oar itself, the whole thing named for its flat end
anagram fodder, the other five letters

explanation.surface: A rower carrying his blade through a rough part of Genoa.
explanation.walkthrough: A blade is an oar in rowing slang, and that is the piece most easily missed, because 'carrying blade' reads as a knife and the evening news. The Italian port supplies only five of the eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-go area is a district the police and outsiders will not enter, which is what makes it the dangerous neighbourhood wanted here.

clue.text: A broken-hearted Wimbledon champion had to annul

indicators.note: the heart of the word, its middle pair of letters, is broken up and rearranged

parts.note: Björn Borg won the Wimbledon men's singles five times in a row, 1976 to 1980
ate means had, as in had a meal

explanation.surface: A tennis star left devastated after being forced to cancel something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken-hearted' scrambles the middle OR of BORG to give BROG; A comes before it and ATE after.
explanation.definitionFit: To abrogate a law or agreement is to repeal or cancel it formally, a synonym of annul.

clue.text: Obsessive hiding front of fashion mag with hands

definitions.note: 'With hands' describes a clock face instead of naming a thing, and the answer is the adjective for precisely that kind of dial, so the phrase stands in for it.

parts.note: somebody obsessive about small details is anal, in the informal sense borrowed from Freud

indicators.note: What is hiding is out of sight, and the front of a word is the letter it starts with, so that first letter never gets written.

parts.note: Vogue is the fashion magazine, and the word is taken whole before anything goes
the V standing at the front of the magazine's name is the letter kept out of sight

explanation.surface: An obsessive covering the front of a fashion magazine with his hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With hands' is the definition and points at a clock face, not at the pair over the magazine. Vogue is the fashion magazine crosswords reach for, and only its first letter is asked to disappear.
explanation.definitionFit: An analogue clock is the one with hands sweeping round a dial, as against a digital display, which has none.

clue.text: Early forms of life are vital for evolution — it can be forgotten

indicators.note: evolution is gradual change, so the remaining letters change their order
the word it is left out, removed from the two words before

explanation.surface: A remark on natural history: some ingredients are essential for evolution while others can be ignored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be forgotten' removes IT from ARE VITAL, leaving AREVAL, and 'for evolution' rearranges those six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Larvae are the immature young of insects and amphibians, early stages before the adult form.

clue.text: Criticise time taken by BT, getting back on line

indicators.note: What is taken by something is taken into it, so the letters named before go inside the ones after.

parts.note: BT ran Britain's telephones for decades, and the two letters are used exactly as the clue prints them
an era is a stretch of time, the Victorian one or the jet one

indicators.note: The back of a word is the letter it finishes on, so only that last one is picked up.

parts.note: the letter this word ends on

explanation.surface: Complaining about how long the phone company took to get the line working again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting back on line' is what an engineer does in the surface and is worth exactly one letter here. The company's initials are printed in the clue and go straight into the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To berate someone is to scold them loudly and at length, which is criticism delivered to the face rather than written down.

clue.text: The Rock put up revolutionary toy tent

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting a word up means writing it from bottom to top

parts.note: the Rock is the nickname of Gibraltar, shortened to Gib
a top is a toy that spins, revolving on its point

explanation.surface: A wrestler nicknamed The Rock erects a toy tent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' reverses GIB, the Rock of Gibraltar, to BIG. The Rock also suggests the wrestler and actor, which is the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: The big top is the main circus tent where the performance takes place.

clue.text: Woman driven off a cliff when steering mechanism breaks cheers

indicators.note: Something that breaks into a house is inside it a moment later, so the word before goes within the word after.

parts.note: ta is the everyday British thank-you, the one muttered at a bar
the helm is what steers a boat

explanation.surface: A woman going over a cliff edge because the steering gave way.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition needs a film: Thelma & Louise ends with the two of them driving out over the edge of a canyon rather than surrendering. 'Cheers' is the thanks, not the toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Thelma is half of Thelma & Louise, and the last shot of that film is their car leaving the cliff, which is how the clue names her.

clue.text: Boisterous Irish returned, supporting a band

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the abbreviation is read in reverse

parts.note: pro means in favour of, supporting
a ring is a circular band

explanation.surface: A rowdy Irish fan comes back to cheer on a music group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reverses IR to RI. 'band' suggests musicians, but it is a ring, as on a finger.
explanation.definitionFit: Rip-roaring means wildly noisy and energetic, so it suits something boisterous.

clue.text: Rose sounded triumphant, making a hundred grand

indicators.note: the first letter given is made into the second, swapping one for the other

parts.note: crew is an old past tense of crow, to boast or exult
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: A rose that cheered noisily after earning a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' turns the C of CREW into G. 'Rose' looks like a flower but is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: Grew and rose are both past tenses meaning increased or went up in size.

clue.text: Property found in toilet at Selfridges returned

indicators.note: What is found in something was sitting inside it all along, so the letters run unbroken through the words named.
Something returned comes back the way it came, so that run is read from its far end to its near one.

parts.note: six letters in an unbroken row, starting inside the first word and stopping inside the last

explanation.surface: Something valuable turning up in the loo at Selfridges and being handed back.
explanation.walkthrough: Selfridges is the Oxford Street department store, which is all the surface needs of it. The letters are there in the clue but not in the order they are printed, which is the extra step.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is property in land and buildings — what an agent sells and what a will leaves behind.

clue.text: 'Up for it' dig MeToo rubbished

indicators.note: To rubbish a thing is to throw it out as worthless, and letters tipped into a bin land in no order at all.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Somebody's dig at the MeToo movement being dismissed as worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the only sign that the first three words are a definition rather than the start of a sentence. A good-time girl or a good-time Charlie is out for pleasure and game for anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Good-time describes the pleasure-seeker who is always ready for a night of it, which is what 'up for it' says in newer slang.
